title: Political participation

blocks.heading: Political participation
blocks.text: Women’s political roles include organisation, advocacy, participation and contributions to public decisions. Namibian women contributed to liberation and independence; subsequent integration into development requires substantive voice as well as recognition. Assess influence and access, not presence alone.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Liberation and independence
blocks.text: Women participated in Namibia’s liberation and independence struggle and in building political and social organisations. Recognition of past participation can challenge claims that public activity belongs to men, but historical contribution does not itself establish present equal influence.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: National development
blocks.text: Integrating women into development includes access to resources, planning, skills and decisions across programmes. Consulting women after priorities and budgets are fixed offers less influence than participation while those decisions remain open.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Formal and factual equality
blocks.text: Formal equality concerns equal rules or recognised rights; factual inequality concerns unequal lived access or outcomes. Identify the practical barrier and evidence. Unequal outcomes alone do not isolate one cause, but equal written rules alone do not disprove a barrier.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Promoting rights
blocks.text: Promoting women’s rights can involve information, advocacy, accessible services and accountability for fair treatment. A right is more usable when people know it and can reach an effective response to exclusion. Do not invent a current legal procedure from a general principle.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: A practical access test
blocks.text: Explain which political-participation arrangement better supports influence: an invented council adds women to a meeting after its budget is fixed; another gives diverse participants access to budget decisions while options remain open. The second offers more substantive influence because participants can affect the allocation. Extra attendance in the first is recognition but does not reopen the decision; assess whether input can actually change priorities.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: A dated national context
blocks.text: A 1997 UN account of Namibia’s reporting described equal political participation and measures aimed at representation. Treat it as historical evidence, not a current legal guide: [UN meeting account](https://press.un.org/en/1997/19970708.wom976.html). The syllabus’s distinction between formal equality and lived inequality still requires access and influence evidence.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Connect to traditional roles (6.1), education (7.3) and research (10.1). Use evidence about resources, voice and practical access. Fictional cases do not establish current law, service availability or a diagnosis about any individual.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
